title: Complete shortest-word classification for two distinct involutions of finite product order
statement:
Let $G$ be a group, meaning a set with associative multiplication, identity $1$ and two-sided inverses, and let $s,t\in G$ satisfy $s
e1$, $t
e1$, $s
e t$ and $s^2=t^2=1$. Suppose $st$ has finite order $m$, meaning $m$ is the least positive integer such that $(st)^m=1$. Put $S=\{s,t\}$, a finite set [def-sfb-finite-infinite-set]. Let $H$ be the subgroup of all finite products of elements of $S$, and let $d(u)$ be the least length of such a word with product $u\in H$. Write $B_s(k)$ and $B_t(k)$ for the alternating words of length $k$ in the alphabet $\{s,t\}$ beginning with $s$ and $t$, respectively, and let $b_s(k)$ and $b_t(k)$ be their products. Both words of length $0$ are empty. Then $m\ge2$, and the following list contains every element of $H$ exactly once: $$1,\quad b_s(k),b_t(k)\ (1\le k<m),\quad w_0,$$ where $w_0=b_s(m)=b_t(m)$. One has $d(1)=0$, $d(b_s(k))=d(b_t(k))=k$ for $1\le k<m$, and $d(w_0)=m$. The only shortest word for $1$ is the empty word; the only shortest word for $b_s(k)$, respectively $b_t(k)$, with $1\le k<m$, is $B_s(k)$, respectively $B_t(k)$; the only shortest words for $w_0$ are $B_s(m)$ and $B_t(m)$. No deletion condition or presentation of $G$ is assumed.

proof.text: Put $r=st$. Since $r=1$ would give $t=s^{-1}=s$, one has $m\ge2$. For each integer $n$, divide $n=qm+j$ with $0\le j<m$; then $r^n=r^j$. Minimality of $m$ gives $r^n=1$ if and only if $j=0$. Consequently $r^a=r^b$ if and only if $m$ divides $a-b$. This uses only $r^m=1$ and cancellation; negative powers mean powers of $r^{-1}$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 1.

proof.text: The involution equations give $r^{-1}=ts$ and $srs=ts=r^{-1}$. The element $s$ is not any power of $r$: if $s=r^a$, it commutes with $r$, so $r=srs=r^{-1}$ and $r^2=1$. Step 1 then gives $m=2$. Reducing $a$ modulo $2$ gives $s=1$ or $s=r$; the former is excluded and the latter gives $t=s^{-1}r=1$, also excluded. Hence $r^a\ne r^b s$ for all integers $a,b$, since such an equality would put $s=r^{a-b}$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 2.

proof.text:
Pair adjacent letters in each alternating word. For $a\ge0$ its product is
$$b_s(2a)=r^a,\qquad b_t(2a)=r^{-a},\qquad b_s(2a+1)=r^a s,\qquad b_t(2a+1)=r^{-(a+1)}s.$$
Indeed the even cases are $(st)^a$ and $(ts)^a$; the odd cases append $s$ and $t$, respectively, and $t=r^{-1}s$. For $m=2a$ the two length-$m$ products agree because their exponents differ by $m$; for $m=2a+1$ the odd formulas give the same conclusion. Call this common element $w_0$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 3.

proof.text: Consider alternating words of lengths $k,l\le m$. Opposite length parities cannot have equal products by step 2. With equal parity and the same initial letter, the exponent difference in step 3 has absolute value $|k-l|/2<m$, so step 1 forces $k=l$. With opposite initial letters the absolute exponent difference is $(k+l)/2$. If at least one word is nonempty, this is positive and at most $m$; it is divisible by $m$ exactly when $k+l=2m$, hence $k=l=m$. The empty word is represented by either initial-letter convention at length zero and is the single exception with difference zero. Thus among these words the only equal products come from the identical word, the two empty-word conventions, or the two length-$m$ words. In particular none of the positive-length words of length at most $m$ represents $1$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 4.

proof.text: Deleting an adjacent $ss$ or $tt$ preserves the product and reduces length by $2$. A word with no such pair alternates, since its alphabet has exactly the distinct letters $s,t$. If an alternating word has length $n>m$, replace its first $m$ letters by the other alternating length-$m$ block, using step 3. The final letter of the replaced block changes to the opposite letter. This new final letter equals the next letter of the original word, since that next letter was opposite to the old final letter. Delete this equal adjacent pair. The resulting word has the same product and length $n-2$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 5.

proof.text: Starting with any word, apply step 5 whenever it has an equal adjacent pair or is alternating of length greater than $m$. Each application reduces its nonnegative integer length by $2$, so the process terminates at an alternating word of length at most $m$ (possibly empty). Every element of $H$ has a word by its definition, and hence occurs in the displayed list. Step 4 proves that the list has no repetitions after the two length-$m$ products are recorded just once as $w_0$.

source.place: Agent-written cancellation and exponent calculation, steps 1–7; comparison only: Cashen, Chapter 2 §1, printed pp.27–29, Lemma 1.0.1 and Theorem 1.0.2. Local source WANTED. Step 6.

proof.text: A shortest word exists for each $u\in H$ by taking the least of its nonempty set of representing lengths. Step 5 shows that every shortest word alternates and has length at most $m$. If $u=b_s(k)$ or $b_t(k)$ with $1\le k<m$, step 4 forces such a shortest word to be the corresponding word $B_s(k)$ or $B_t(k)$, respectively; therefore its length is $k$ and it is unique. For $u=w_0$, step 4 forces length $m$ and initial letter $s$ or $t$. Both displayed length-$m$ words represent $u$, and both are shortest. For $u=1$, the empty word has length $0$, and every word of length $0$ is that same empty word. These give all asserted metric values and all shortest-word classifications.
